(iv) If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.5

[9] I find that the evidence in items A-E above does not meet the test for new evidence. Although the two declarations (items A-B) are dated XXXX XXXX, 2022, the contents of these declarations are about the dispute which happened in 2016 over ancestral land. I find that this evidence did not arise after the rejection of their claims for refugee protections; it was available at the time of the RPD Decision; and given that the central allegations of risk in India are due to the land dispute, it was reasonable to expect them to provide this evidence to the RPD before the decision was made.

[10] The two-news articles (items C-D) pre-date the RPD Decision and the Human Right Watch report (item E) is for 2020. I find that the evidence (items C-D) did not arise after the rejection of their claims for refugee protection, and it was available at the time of the RPD Decision. Regarding the Human Rights Watch report, I note that Immigration and Refugee Board National Documentation Package for India, dated June 30, 2022, contains the latest Human Right Watch report dated 2022 which I am obliged to consider in my assessment.

[11] In summary, I find that the Appellants did not establish the evidence in items A-E above either arose after the rejection of their claims for refugee protection, or this evidence was not available at the time of the RPD Decision, or why they could not reasonably have been expected, in the circumstances, to bring the evidence to the RPD before the decision was made. Therefore, items A-E above will not be accepted into this appeal.
The evidence submitted by the Appellants in F-G above is accepted.

In my review of items F-G, I note that for item F the printout date is noted as XXXX 2022, but this does not demonstrate the document was not available at the time of the hearing. Nonetheless, I will give the Appellants the benefit of doubt. I find that items F-G arose after the RPD's rejection of their claims. I also find that this evidence is new, credible, and relevant. Thus, this evidence is accepted into the record.

27...The claimants hold Special Resident Retiree Visas (SRRV) that is a non-immigrant visa issued by the Government of the Philippines. According to information available from the website of the Embassy of the Philippines in Norway, SRRV grants non-immigrant status to visa holder.
The visas are linked to an investment and the holders of the permits have mostly tax benefits and do not have any of the rights that are associated with being a citizen on (sic) the Philippines.
The holder of SRRV cannot even buy real property in the Philippines. The claimants have already commenced the process of surrendering their SRRV visas. A copy of the letter from the claimants' lawyers in the Philippines is attached as Exhibit 9.9

[21] I note that paragraphs 3(3)(g) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules10 (RAD Rules) requires the Appellants' Memorandum to include full and detailed submissions on various aspects of the appeal. [22] I find that the Appellant's submissions regarding the RPD's exclusion findings do not comply with either of the aforementioned paragraphs because the Appellants do not identify in their Memorandum the sections of the RPD's reasons they consider to be problematic, and more particularly, the Appellants do not even address the conclusions reached by the RPD are erroneous or specify the errors committed by the RPD related to the exclusion finding.

[23] The jurisprudence supports that it is not the role of the RAD to search or guess for potential errors that the RPD may have committed.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] The Appellants, XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and her husband XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant), and their children XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX (Minor Associate Appellants), citizens of India, appeal the Decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated May 31, 2022, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

[2] The Appellants are permanent residents of the Philippines. In the Philippines, the Appellants fear members of the Abu Sayyaf, a terrorist group in the Philippines and XXXX who they allege is associated with Abu Sayyaf.
[3] In India, the Appellants fear the Principal Appellant's brother because of a land dispute between the Principal Appellant and her brother.

[4] The RPD rejected their claims for refugee protection on the basis that the Appellants were excluded pursuant to section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1 and Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (UN Refugee Convention).2
DECISION

[5] I dismiss the Appellants' appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are excluded under section 98 of the IRPA and Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention. Therefore, the Appellants are not Convention3 refugees nor persons in need of protection.
NEW EVIDENCE

[6] The Appellants have submitted the following as new evidence:
A) Declaration of XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2022.
B) Declaration of XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2022.
C) News article: "What Happens When a Billion Identities Are Digitized?", Yale Insights, March 27, 2020.
D) India 2020 Human Rights Report
E) News article, "Forcing confession by torture rampant in country, first of its kind report reveals", India Today, updated December 10, 2017.
F) Special Resident Retiree's Visa, from the website of the Philippine Embassy in Oslo.
G) Letter regarding cancellation of Special Resident Retiree's Visa from law firm, XXXX XXXX & Associates, dated XXXX XXXX, 2022.
The evidence submitted by the Appellants in A-E above is rejected

[7] According to the Law,4 I can only accept evidence that:
(i) arose after the RPD decision; or
(ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
(iii) that could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring it to the RPD before the decision.
(iv) If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.5

[8] The Appellants state that they are submitting new evidence and are requesting an oral hearing. The Appellants have not provided any submissions on how the evidence, items A-G above, meet the test for new evidence.

[9] I find that the evidence in items A-E above does not meet the test for new evidence. Although the two declarations (items A-B) are dated XXXX XXXX, 2022, the contents of these declarations are about the dispute which happened in 2016 over ancestral land. I find that this evidence did not arise after the rejection of their claims for refugee protections; it was available at the time of the RPD Decision; and given that the central allegations of risk in India are due to the land dispute, it was reasonable to expect them to provide this evidence to the RPD before the decision was made.

[10] The two-news articles (items C-D) pre-date the RPD Decision and the Human Right Watch report (item E) is for 2020. I find that the evidence (items C-D) did not arise after the rejection of their claims for refugee protection, and it was available at the time of the RPD Decision. Regarding the Human Rights Watch report, I note that Immigration and Refugee Board National Documentation Package for India, dated June 30, 2022, contains the latest Human Right Watch report dated 2022 which I am obliged to consider in my assessment.

[11] In summary, I find that the Appellants did not establish the evidence in items A-E above either arose after the rejection of their claims for refugee protection, or this evidence was not available at the time of the RPD Decision, or why they could not reasonably have been expected, in the circumstances, to bring the evidence to the RPD before the decision was made. Therefore, items A-E above will not be accepted into this appeal.
The evidence submitted by the Appellants in F-G above is accepted.

[12] The Appellants did not provide any submissions about how items F-G meets the test for new evidence under section 110(4)6 of the IRPA. In my review of items F-G, I note that for item F the printout date is noted as XXXX 2022, but this does not demonstrate the document was not available at the time of the hearing. Nonetheless, I will give the Appellants the benefit of doubt. I find that items F-G arose after the RPD's rejection of their claims. I also find that this evidence is new, credible, and relevant. Thus, this evidence is accepted into the record.

[13] The Appellants have requested an oral hearing before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). Section 110(6)7 of the IRPA provides that the RAD may hold a hearing only if the RAD has accepted new evidence on appeal which raises serious issues of credibility. Since the evidence accepted in this appeal does not raise serious issues of credibility, the request for an oral hearing is denied.
JURISPRUDENTIAL GUIDE

[14] In my analysis, I have considered and applied the reasoning in Jurisprudential Guide MB8-00025 which confirms the preferred interpretation of Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention. The Jurisprudential Guide confirms that allegations of risk in a country of residence are to be taken into consideration in the analysis of whether a refugee claimant is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E.
ANALYSIS
[15] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.8

[16] I have considered their submissions and conducted my own independent assessment of the evidence. I find that exclusion under section 98 of the IRPA and Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention is determinative of the appeal.
[17] The RPD found the Appellants' allegations of risk to be credible both in the Philippines and in India.

[18] However, the RPD determined that the Appellants were not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The RPD found that as permanent residents of the Philippines, the Appellants had status substantially similar to that of Philippines nationals. Therefore, the RPD determined that they were excluded under Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention.

[19] Regarding the Appellants' risk in the Phillippines, the RPD found the Appellants do not face either a serious possibility of persecution, or a danger of torture or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the Philippines.

[20] The Appellants have not clearly articulated their arguments that the RPD erred in its exclusion analysis nor have they specifically identified the errors. They state at paragraph 27 of the memorandum:
27...The claimants hold Special Resident Retiree Visas (SRRV) that is a non-immigrant visa issued by the Government of the Philippines. According to information available from the website of the Embassy of the Philippines in Norway, SRRV grants non-immigrant status to visa holder.
The visas are linked to an investment and the holders of the permits have mostly tax benefits and do not have any of the rights that are associated with being a citizen on (sic) the Philippines.
The holder of SRRV cannot even buy real property in the Philippines. The claimants have already commenced the process of surrendering their SRRV visas. A copy of the letter from the claimants' lawyers in the Philippines is attached as Exhibit 9.9

[21] I note that paragraphs 3(3)(g) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules10 (RAD Rules) requires the Appellants' Memorandum to include full and detailed submissions on various aspects of the appeal. The two relevant subparagraphs which are particularly relevant in this appeal are 3(3)(g)(i),11 the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, and (3)(3)(g)(ii)12 which asks the Appellants to identify specifically where the errors are located in the written reasons of the RPD's Decision that the Appellants are appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the RPD's Hearing.

[22] I find that the Appellant's submissions regarding the RPD's exclusion findings do not comply with either of the aforementioned paragraphs because the Appellants do not identify in their Memorandum the sections of the RPD's reasons they consider to be problematic, and more particularly, the Appellants do not even address the conclusions reached by the RPD are erroneous or specify the errors committed by the RPD related to the exclusion finding.
[23] The jurisprudence supports that it is not the role of the RAD to search or guess for potential errors that the RPD may have committed.
[24] The Federal Court in Dhillon13 states:

[20] ... It is not the RAD's function to supplement the weaknesses of an appeal before it, or, for that matter, of the refugee protection claim presented in the first place. It is not its role to come up with new ideas that might assist appellants in succeeding with their appeal and, ultimately, their refugee claim.
[25] In Dahal,14 the Federal Court states:

[37] By simply satisfying itself that no such additional errors were made, the RAD's decision should not become vulnerable to being set aside on judicial review, based solely on its general concurrence with findings made by the RPD in respect of matters that were not raised on appeal by the Applicants. In my view, this would largely vitiate the purpose of Rule 3(3)(g) of the Rules, which requires an appellant to identify (i) the errors that are the grounds of appeal, and (ii) where those errors are located in the RPD's decision or in the transcript recording of its hearing.

[26] In any event, in my independent assessment of the record, I reviewed the RPD's exclusion findings. I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellants were excluded under section 98 of the IRPA and Article 1E of the UN Refugee Convention for reasons which follow.
Article 1E Exclusion

[27] Article 1E reads as follows:
1E. This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

[28] Article 1E is incorporated in section 98 of the IRPA which reads:
Exclusion - Refugee Convention
98 A person referred in section E or F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
[29] In Zeng,15 the Federal Court of Appeal described the three-part test applicable to determine if a person is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention:

[28] [1] Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded. If the answer is no, [2] the next question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E. If the answer is yes, [3] the RPD must consider and balance various factors. These include, but are not limited to, the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary), whether the claimant could return to the third country, the risk the claimant would face in the home country, Canada's international obligations, and any other relevant facts [RAD emphasis added].

[30] In Shamlou,16 the Federal Court considered the rights and obligations set out in Article 1E and held that these include the right to return, the right to work freely without restrictions, the right to study, and full access to social services.
Appellants have permanent resident status in the Philippines

[31] I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants had a permanent resident status at the time of the RPD hearing and continued to have this status at the time they filed their appeal to the RAD. The Appellants provided a letter, dated XXXX XXXX, 2022, from a law firm in the Philippines which indicates that they are in the process of cancelling the Appellants' SRRV status in the Philippines. The Appellants have not provided any evidence to the RAD that their status, since XXXX 2022, has been cancelled. In any event, the relevant date for my assessment of the Appellants' status is the date of the RPD Hearing and not events which occurred afterwards.

[32] At the RPD Hearing, the Principal Appellant testified that she was a permanent resident of the Philippines. The Associate Appellant and their children's SRRVs have no expiration date. Instead, their SRRVs expiry is indicated "indefinite."17

[33] As such, I see no error in the RPD findings that the Appellants, at the time of the RPD hearing, had permanent resident status in the Philippines. Therefore, I confirm these findings of the RPD.
Appellants had the rights and obligations same as nationals of the Philippines
[34] The RPD found that the Appellants' permanent resident status conferred them rights similar to that of nationals of the Philippines.
[35] The Appellants are challenging they are unable to own property in the Philippines which they believe is a right that nationals of the Philippines have.

[36] After conducting my independent assessment of the evidence, I note that the Associate Appellant was self-employed and operated his own business XXXX XXXX while the Principal Appellant was a housewife. As permanent residents of the Philippines, they made trips abroad and had the right to return to the Philippines. For example, the Principal Appellant travelled to India and returned to the Philippines. The Associate Appellant as well as their children also travelled to Japan and returned to the Philippines.

[37] Though the issue of the right to study or have access to social services including health care were not canvassed at the RPD Hearing, the Appellants have not provided any actual or concrete evidence that they were not able to access social services including health care or education.

[38] Before the RAD, the Appellants submit that as permanent residents of the Philippines they are unable to own real property, this issue was not raised before the RPD. I note that the Associate Appellant owned and operated his own business in the Philippines. Though the issue of whether the Appellants owned a home in the Philippines was not canvassed at the RPD Hearing, the Appellants did not provide any evidence that they either did or did not.

[39] In any event, the Appellants have provided no authority to support that the rights and obligations attached to nationality of the country, as described in Article 1E of the Refugee Convention and Shamulou above, includes a right to own property. As noted above, Shamlou described the rights and obligations as the right to return to the country, the right to work freely, the right to study, and full access to social services. There is no mention of a right to real property ownership including a home ownership. It appears from Shamlou that the more important considerations are the ability to return, live, study, and support oneself in the country, rather being able to purchase property.

[40] I find that in the Appellants' circumstances, they can live, work, and study, and have been able to leave and return to the Philippines. Thus, their status as permanent residents has provided them with the rights and obligations of nationals, even though they are unable to own real property.

[41] Therefore, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that as permanent residents of the Philippines, the Appellants enjoyed the same rights and obligations as nationals of the Philippines.
Appellants do not face a serious possibility of persecution or likely risk of harm in the Philippines

[42] The Principal Appellant was kidnapped by a member of Abu Sayyaf for ransom on XXXX XXXX, 2016. She was released several days later upon payment of the ransom. The Appellants state they will be killed by Abu Sayyaf or by XXXX who is associated with Abu Sayyaf.

[43] At the RPD Hearing, the Associate Appellant testified that when he learnt that his wife had been kidnapped, he reported it to the police. The police took his complaint and started a search. However, he paid the ransom, and the kidnappers released his wife.

[44] The RPD accepted their allegations of risk as credible. However, the RPD found that the Appellants do not face either a serious possibility of persecution or likely risk of harm in the Philippines. The RPD found that the risk no longer existed because Abu Sayyaf's size and power had decreased significantly since 2016 and no longer posed a risk to them. Regarding the risk from XXXX the RPD found that there was no evidence that XXXX remained interested in them or was affiliated with the militant group. The Appellants do not challenge these findings of the RPD.

[45] After conducting my own independent assessment of the evidence, I do not see any errors in the RPD's analysis. Therefore, I confirm the findings of the RPD that there was no longer a risk to the Appellants because Abu Sayyaf's size and power had decreased significantly since 2016, and there was no evidence that XXXX remained interested in the Appellants or was still affiliated with Abu Sayyaf.
SUMMARY

[46] The RPD also correctly concluded that the Appellants are excluded from refugee protection as they had the benefits of a form of safe surrogate protection in the Philippines where their permanent resident status gave them access to substantially the same rights and obligations as nationals of that country. As part of its Article 1E analysis, the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellants did not establish that they would face a serious possibility of persecution or likely risk of harm in the Philippines.
CONCLUSION
[47] I find that the Appellants are excluded from refugee protection by the combined effect of Article 1E of the Convention and section 98 of the IRPA.

[48] I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
